advice.text:
"Thank you," he said, and asked after a cheap bed and a meal, and whether anyone bought beetle chitin.

The keeper pulled her ledger back toward herself and tapped the counter with one blunt finger, thinking.

"Rest and eat — the Drowned Ox, two streets down toward the river. Sign's a drowned ox, can't miss it. Marta keeps it. A bed's three coppers, stew's one, and she doesn't ask questions of Guild folk with blood on them, which you'll want today. There's cheaper rooms by the tanneries, but you'll sleep worse for it, so I'd not bother."

She leaned a forearm on the counter and looked at the pouch at his hip.

"Chitin — yes. Hessel the smith, on Cooper's Lane, buys crystal beetle plates off adventurers. He tempers them into scale fittings, lamp backs, things like that. F-rank plate he'll give you a copper or two a piece, maybe three if they're uncracked, which yours won't be." A glance at his torn sleeve. "He'll knock the price for burn marks, so don't expect much."

She paused, then added, "The gland now, that's different. If you've a venom gland off one of those, don't sell it to a smith. The academy buys those — there's a steward at the cleft, or the apothecary on Chandler's Row takes them and sells them on. Worth real money, more than the whole cull paid. Keep it dry."

She straightened and took up her pen again.

"Drowned Ox. Hessel for plates, Chandler's Row for the gland. And eat something before you fall over on my floor."

fen.text:
Two streets toward the river, and each of them longer than it should have been. Glassmere went about its dinner hour around him — smell of onions from a doorway, a dog trotting past with a string of sausage in its mouth, someone shouting for a boy named Pip — and he walked through it with his staff as a walking stick, leaving small dark spots on the cobbles when he forgot to hold his forearm still.

The Drowned Ox stood where the street bent down to the water: a low timbered front, the sign swinging above the door, a carved ox upside-down in painted waves, gone green with weather. Inside it was dim and warm, smelling of peat smoke, spilled ale and boiling meat. A few locals at the long tables, a pair of carters arguing quietly over a ledger, a girl stacking bowls.

Marta was the woman behind the bar — thick-armed, gray-streaked hair pinned back, a ladle in one hand like she'd been born holding it. She looked at him coming in: the torn robes, the dried blood, the staff.

"Guild cull, is it?" She nodded at the bench nearest the fire before he'd said a word. "Sit. Stew's coming."

He took the bed for the day along with the meal, and she counted the four coppers out of his hand without ceremony, biting one of them out of habit. The stew came in a wooden bowl big enough to bathe in — barley, turnip, some dark meat, bread on the side — and the heat of it in his hands was nearly as good as the eating.

The room she gave him was under the eaves, narrow: a straw bed, a hook for the staff, a shuttered window over the river. Marta set a jug of water on the sill.

"You'll want that wound looked at," she said from the door. "Old Fen does stitching, two doors down, costs a copper or two. Or sleep and hope. Your choice."

She pulled the door to behind her. Downstairs, the carters had gone back to arguing.

price.text:
Doss snorted and went back to his leaves, tipping them from the scale pan into a stoppered jar. "Plates. No. That's smith's work — Hessel tempers them into scale fittings and lamp backs, and he's got the forge for it. I'd have no use for the stuff past grinding a little into poultice grit, and for that I'd pay you a copper a plate at most, which would be insulting us both."

He corked the jar and set it with its brothers. "Take them to Cooper's Lane while the lamps are still lit. He'll weigh them fair if they're whole — mind, he pays less for cracked or scorched ones, so don't let him tell you burn marks came with the beetle. Plate chitin comes off them clean if the killing was."

The ink-stained fingers drummed once on the counter. "Four plates, is it? From the same cull as the gland. That'll be a few silver in your pocket before bedtime, if his evening mood is a good one." He picked his leaves back up and bent to his sorting. "Anything else, or good evening?"

inputs.input: The smithy is shut until tomorrow, so I'll find a cheap inn, get supper and a bed for the night, and come back to Hessel's in the morning.
I'll take the stew and the loft bed — ten copper — then settle in for the night.
I sleep through the night in the loft, then head to Hessel's smithy first thing in the morning.
I knock on the barred door. "Morning — I've paid Hessel forty silver for the jerkin he's fitting for me. When's he back?"
"The jerkin on the peg is mine — I paid your father forty silver yesterday and he cut the straps for it. Can I collect it once the fire's drawn? I'll wait right here."

"Leave my name with him, then — Alaric Red, paid forty silver yesterday for the boiled-leather jerkin he fitted. Tell him I'll call back tomorrow." I leave the boy and head for Chandler's Row to see Sela about selling my slime gel.
"Good morning — I'm selling, not bleeding. I've got five measures of fresh slime gel. What will you pay for them?"
It seems my gel's gone missing somewhere between the cellars and here — I won't waste your time. Actually, would you know anyone who'd buy a bog strider chitin plate?
I thank Sela, wrap the chitin plate in my cloak, and head for the smithy off Ironmonger street to ask what they'll pay for it.
I unwrap the plate and hand it over. "Hinge's still on it and whole as far as I know — I took it off the strider myself. Check it and pay me what it's worth."
"Eleven with the straps, then — deal." I take the coins and the straps.
I strap the greave straps onto my shins to test the fit, then ask Mara what she'd charge to fit them onto a proper pair of lacquered shin-guards like the ones on her wall.
